passage:
Zeenat's notebook had a column for every morning since January: distance, time, how she felt. On the dirt road past the sugarcane fields, she ran before the azaan finished and was back before her brothers woke.
The district meet was over now. She'd won silver. For two days she felt light. By the third she was pacing the courtyard, tapping her fingers, asking Abbu when the state trials were.
'Beta, rest a week,' he said.
'A week is too long.'
That evening her cousin Mehak came over with henna cones for Friday's wedding. 'You'll come to the mehendi, na? You missed my engagement for practice.'
Zeenat opened her mouth to say she had a long run that night. Then she saw Mehak's face, hopeful and a little braced.
'I'll come,' she said, and closed the notebook.

qa.q: What did Zeenat record in her notebook each morning?
qa.a: Distance, time and how she felt.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat pacing the courtyard by the third day?
qa.a: Without a new target she felt restless and bored, already hungry for the state trials.

qa.q: What choice did Zeenat make when Mehak asked about the mehendi, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She chose to go instead of doing a long run, making room for a relationship that her training had been crowding out.

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about Zeenat's training?
qa.a: Mehak seems hopeful but braced for another no, since Zeenat already missed the engagement for practice.

grounding: Shows a teenager who tracks goals and feels restless without a target, and a moment where she makes room for a relationship her drive had been crowding out.

passage:
Hana's desk in the Toronto apartment had three charts taped above it: violin minutes, maths scores, days until the music school audition. Each evening she coloured in one more square, and the small click of finishing felt better than anything else in her day.
On Saturday, Rafael texted a photo of everyone at the lake. 'Come? One afternoon.'
She wrote back, 'Can't, practice,' like she always did.
On Monday she got a B on a chemistry quiz. She sat very still at lunch, pushing rice around her container. 'I'm nothing if I can't even do this,' she said quietly.
Rafael frowned. 'You're my friend who makes up songs about the bus driver. That's not a grade.'
Hana laughed despite herself, then stopped. She couldn't remember the last time she'd done something just for fun.

qa.q: What were the three charts above Hana's desk?
qa.a: Violin minutes, maths scores and days until the music school audition.

qa.q: What does Hana saying 'I'm nothing if I can't even do this' reveal?
qa.a: It reveals she feels worthless after one B, because she has started measuring her whole worth by results.

qa.q: What moment could become a turning point for Hana, and what might she choose next?
qa.a: Realising she can't remember doing anything just for fun could lead her to say yes to the next afternoon at the lake.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel after hearing 'Can't, practice' again and again?
qa.a: Rafael may feel pushed aside and a little worried, missing the friend who makes up songs about the bus driver.

grounding: Shows a teenager driven by goals and charts whose sense of worth has narrowed to success while rest and friendship are neglected.

passage: People think I'm just competitive. I'm Suraj, Class 11. I've got a whiteboard in my room with every goal on it: 95 in physics, a mile under six minutes, forty books this year. I tick them off. It feels amazing for about a day. Then, honestly, I get restless, like I'm wasting time if there's no next target. Last month I missed my best friend Sabina's birthday because I was doing a mock test. She didn't say much. She just stopped saving me a seat at lunch. That's when I noticed: I've got a whiteboard full of ticks, and I can't remember the last time I just sat with someone. So I added a new line to the board: Sunday afternoons, no goals. It's the hardest one on there.

qa.q: How many books does Suraj want to read this year?
qa.a: Forty books.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel when there is no next target?
qa.a: Suraj feels restless, as if time is being wasted.

qa.q: What small step did Suraj take to balance drive and relationships?
qa.a: Adding "Sunday afternoons, no goals" to the whiteboard.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Suraj missed her birthday?
qa.a: Sabina was probably hurt, which is why she stopped saving a seat at lunch.

grounding: Shows a teen driven by goals and restless without a target, noticing that a friendship has been neglected.

passage:
January: Trisha made a chart: swim twenty lengths without stopping by March, top three in the district by June. Every evening she logged her times. When her brother Vijay asked her to watch a film, she said, "No time."
April: She hit twenty lengths two weeks early. That night she felt restless rather than happy, and wrote a new target before bed. She'd stopped going to her friend's Saturday lunches.
June, after the district meet: She came fourth. She sat in the car, silent, feeling worthless. Vijay handed her a samosa. "You swam your best time ever. Also, you've been missing. We miss you." She looked out at the rain, then leaned against his shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Trisha finish at the district meet?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after coming fourth?
qa.a: She felt worthless, as if the result was the only measure of her.

qa.q: How did Vijay help Trisha?
qa.a: He pointed out her best time and told her the family missed her, reminding her she is more than a result.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay when Trisha keeps saying "No time"?
qa.a: Vijay probably feels shut out and misses his sister.

grounding: Shows over months a goal-driven teen whose worth becomes tied to results as rest and relationships slip.

passage: You set targets like I did, beta. At fifteen I had a notebook of goals: first in class, state chess, a hundred push-ups. I ticked them all. And each time I felt a flat hunger instead of joy, and wrote a bigger one. My friend Sharmila used to come by with raw mangoes and salt, and I'd send her away: "Studying." One day she stopped coming. In the board exam I came first in the district. My photo was in the newspaper. I, Eshaan, sat alone in my room with that newspaper and felt nothing. That was my turning point. I walked to Sharmila's house with salt and two mangoes. She laughed at me for an hour. I still set goals. I also keep Sundays for mangoes.

qa.q: What did Sharmila bring when she visited?
qa.a: Raw mangoes and salt.

qa.q: What did young Eshaan feel sitting with the newspaper?
qa.a: Eshaan felt empty, with nothing, despite coming first in the district.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Feeling nothing after the success made Eshaan walk to Sharmila's house with mangoes, choosing friendship again.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when she was sent away again and again?
qa.a: Sharmila likely felt hurt and unwanted, so she stopped coming.

grounding: Shows a goal-driven teen for whom success became the only measure until its emptiness led back to a friendship.

passage:
The whole family had arrived for Diwali, and the house was loud with cousins, crackers and pressure cookers. Rukmini sat in the corner with her goal chart: 50 physics problems by Sunday, 45 done.
She'd hit every target this term. When she didn't have one, she felt restless and bored, pacing the room.
Her phone buzzed. Varun: "you coming to my birthday thing tonight?? you said yes last week"
She'd forgotten. Again. That made it three missed plans this month.
Rukmini stared at the chart. Five problems left. Her chest tightened; stopping felt like failing.
Her cousin Leela peeked in. "Are you ever just happy, didi? Or only when you finish?"
Rukmini didn't answer. Then, slowly, she put the chart down, typed "coming, 20 mins," and went to find a clean kurta. The five problems could wait until tomorrow.

qa.q: How many physics problems had Rukmini done by the time Varun messaged?
How did Rukmini feel when she thought about stopping?
qa.a: She felt tense and uneasy, with her chest tightening, because stopping felt like failing.

qa.q: What did Rukmini risk by focusing only on her targets?
qa.a: She risked her friendships, having missed three plans this month, and making success the only measure of her worth.

qa.q: How might Varun feel if Rukmini missed his birthday too?
qa.a: Varun might feel hurt and unimportant, since she had said yes last week and had already missed other plans.

grounding: Shows a goal-driven teen who feels restless without targets, and who starts to notice friendships slipping when success is all that counts.
